subject: biology
title: Selection & Genetic Drift Adventure
welcome_lead: Today you'll explore how selection shifts allele frequencies — directional, stabilising and disruptive — plus drift.
meta_desc: A-Level Biology Evolution — directional, stabilising, disruptive selection, genetic drift, founder effect and population bottlenecks.
final_note: You learned the three types of natural selection, how genetic drift acts randomly in small populations, and how founder effect and bottleneck events reduce variation.

concepts.def: One extreme favoured — mean shifts (e.g. antibiotic resistance)
Mean favoured, extremes selected against (e.g. human birth weight)
Both extremes favoured — can lead to two populations
Random change in allele frequencies — strong in small populations
Small group founds new population — limited gene pool
Sudden severe reduction in population → loss of variation

walkthroughs.body_html:
Selection reshapes allele frequencies in different ways.

Directional selection — environment changes; one extreme is fittest. Mean phenotype shifts.
Example: dark peppered moths during industrial revolution.

Stabilising selection — both extremes selected against. Reduces variation around the mean.
Example: human birth weight ~3.5 kg is optimal.

Disruptive selection — both extremes favoured, intermediate selected against. Can split a population.

Selection is about fitness. Genetic drift is about luck.

By chance, some individuals contribute more alleles to the next generation. In a large population this evens out. In a small population, allele frequencies can swing wildly — and rare alleles may be lost altogether.

Drift acts faster than selection in small populations.

Founder effect — a few individuals colonise a new area. Their alleles are not representative of the source population.
Example: Afrikaner population in South Africa has high frequency of Huntington's disease allele.

Bottleneck — disaster wipes out most of a population (hunting, disease, climate). Survivors carry only a fraction of the original alleles.
Example: cheetahs — genetic similarity across the species reflects ancient bottlenecks.

Both reduce genetic variation — making populations more vulnerable.
